resources.string: Winning tips
Quick ideas you can use in your very next game
Each tip takes about 30 seconds. Pick one idea, try it in your next game, and come back when it starts to feel natural.
Basics
Step up
Expert level
These are easier to understand after the earlier tips feel natural. You can read them anytime, but there is no need to learn them first.
For your next game
Previous
Next
Take fewer discs early
Early in the game, choose moves that flip fewer discs.
Flipping many discs early exposes more of your discs and gives the opponent more choices. Keep your discs compact and flip as little as you can.
Do not pick the move that flips the most. Look for a smaller flip.
Outlined: 1 disc. ×: 4 discs.\nEarly on, choose the smaller flip.
Reduce your opponent’s choices
A strong move reduces the opponent’s options.
Do not focus on how many discs you flip. Look at how many legal moves the opponent gets next. Fewer choices for them means more control for you.
Before you play, ask: “How many moves will they have next?”
Outlined: 4 legal moves for the opponent.\n×: 9 legal moves. Choose the outlined move.
Take a corner when you can
If a corner is available, take it.
A corner disc can never be flipped. Taking a corner also gives you a strong base for securing the nearby edge. Check corners first.
If you can play a corner, take the corner first.
The outlined corner is available.\nTake the corner in this position.
Stay off the diagonal next to an empty corner
Do not play diagonally next to an empty corner.
Playing on that diagonal square gives the opponent an easy path to the corner. While the corner is empty, stay off that square.
Avoid the diagonal square beside an empty corner.
Playing × at b2 gives the opponent the a1 corner.\nStay off the diagonal beside an empty corner.
Do not rush to the edge
In the opening and midgame, do not rush to the edge.
Going to the edge too early reduces your future choices and makes corners easier for the opponent to attack. Prefer an interior move first.
Choose the interior before the edge.
× goes to the edge. The outline stays inside.\nAt this stage, choose the interior move.
In the endgame, play for the final count
In the endgame, play for the number of discs you will have at the finish.
Early on, keep your disc count low and your options open. Once only a few empty squares remain, switch gears and choose the sequence that leaves you with more discs at the end.
In the endgame, ask: “How many discs will I have at the finish?”
10 empty squares remain.\nFrom here, focus on the final disc count.
Count discs that can never flip
A disc that can no longer flip is yours for the rest of the game.
Corner discs stay yours forever. Same-color edge discs connected to a secured corner are stable too. Count these stable discs in the endgame.
After taking a corner, count the stable discs along its edges.
The outlined corner has already been taken.\nThat disc can never flip again.
Parity: count even and odd empty regions
In the endgame, count whether each empty region has an even or odd number of squares.
When empty squares split into small regions, count the size of each region. Even and odd counts tell you who is set up to make the last move there. Use parity to plan the remaining order of play.
When you see an isolated empty region, count whether it is even or odd.
The outlined top-right region has 2 empty squares.\nIt is an even region.
Count remaining moves, not only discs
In the endgame, count remaining moves before current flips.
Once only a few empty squares remain, count where each side can still play and how many turns are left. Read the sequence first, then choose the current move.
In the endgame, ask “How many moves are left?” before “How many discs flip now?”
Use the outlined empty squares as checkpoints.\nCount the remaining sequence.
